newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil coffee trade stunned by USDA crop estimate.
newsitem.headline: Brazil coffee trade stunned by USDA crop estimate.

text.p: Brazilian coffee traders were shocked by an estimate of the 1997/98 Brazilian coffee crop by U.S. Agriculture Department which puts the crop currently being harvested at above last year's crop.
In its first estimate of the 1997/98 Brazilian crop, the USDA plotted the harvest at 28 million 60-kg bags against 27.5 million in 1996/97.
"What is the most shocking thing is to say there is more coming this year than last. That is totally wrong," said Jorge Esteve, president of the Brazilian Coffee Exporters Association (Abecafe).
"It's certainly not what we expect. It's too high," said John Wolthers of Santos export firm Icatu/Sumatra.
"(The USDA) is the only one (saying the crop will be higher). We contest it," he added.
Icatu/Sumatra currently see the 1997/98 harvest at 24 million bags, down from 27.5 million in 1996/97.
USDA's 1997/98 figure compares with 22 million bags being used by the Brazilian government and trade estimates of 23 million and 25 million bags.
Producers are generally expecting a crop of around 20 million to 22 million bags.
No government or producer officials were immediately available to comment on the 1997/98 estimate.
The USDA's 1996/97 forecast is slightly higher than a 27 million bag estimate issued in December.
For the crop harvested last year, Brazil's government is working with 25 million to 26 million bags while traders generally are of the view that the harvest was from 27 million up to 30 million bags.

USDA's Brazilian estimates have always been watched closely by the world's coffee markets, with its former agronomist Leon Yallouz making 144 trips into the coffee regions before the USDA closed the Rio de Janeiro office last year.
Today's estimate is the first for the new USDA agronomist who traders said visited coffee areas with a Washington-based USDA specialist.
Yallouz is continuing to provide crop forecasts as an independent consultant and his next forecast for private clients will be issued June 20.
His last estimate in February is believed to have been around 27.5 million bags although this has never been confirmed.
Yallouz declined to comment on the USDA's 1997/98 forecast but said he thought the 1996/97 figure was too low.
"(The 1996/97 harvest) was somewhere over 28 million bags," Yallouz said.
